breakfast.name: Burek (Flaky Pastry with Meat)
instructions: Burek is the Serbian breakfast institution -- Balkan flaky pastry with meat
Technically from Ottoman cuisine -- burek spread across the Balkans under the Ottoman Empire
Serbian burek is specifically with minced meat -- not cheese, not spinach (those are different)
The Serbian distinction: burek = meat; with cheese it is gibanica; with spinach, zeljanica
Made with yufka (phyllo-type) sheets brushed with oil
The sheets are filled and rolled, coiled into a round pan (spiral form)
Baked until golden and crispy on the outside
The outside should shatter; the inside should be juicy with meat filling
Pekara (bakery) culture: Serbian pekare open at 4-5am for the morning burek rush
The ritual: burek + yoghurt for breakfast at the pekara counter
Eaten standing up -- the pekara is fast food, not a sit-down place
The yoghurt cuts through the oil of the burek -- essential accompaniment
breakfast.description: Serbian flaky pastry breakfast -- yufka (phyllo-type) sheets coiled with spiced minced meat filling, baked until the outside shatters and the filling stays juicy. Serbian burek specifically means meat; cheese is gibanica; spinach is zeljanica. Pekare (bakeries) open at 4-5am for the morning rush. Eaten standing at the counter with a cup of yoghurt. Ottoman inheritance, completely Serbianized.

breakfast.name: Gibanica (Serbian Cheese Pastry)
ingredients: White cheese (feta-type or fresh Serbian sir)
instructions: Gibanica is the Serbian cheese pastry -- the most beloved Serbian pastry alongside burek
The distinction: gibanica is the cheese version; burek is the meat version
The filling: crumbled white cheese, eggs, and sour cream -- simple and rich
Kajmak (Serbian clotted cream) can be used instead of sour cream -- richer
The yufka sheets are crumpled (not folded neatly) -- this creates the irregular texture
The crumpling technique: unique to gibanica -- the sheets are not carefully layered
The crumpled sheets create pockets that hold the cheese filling
Baked until golden -- the eggs set and bind the cheese
Gibanica is at every Serbian celebration: Easter, Slava (the Serbian patron saint feast)
Slavska pogaca: the special bread at Slava; gibanica: the savory pastry alongside
breakfast.description: Serbian cheese pastry -- yufka (phyllo) sheets crumpled (not neatly layered) and mixed with white cheese, eggs, and sour cream or kajmak (Serbian clotted cream), baked until golden. The crumpling technique creates irregular pockets that hold the filling. At every Serbian celebration: Easter, Slava (patron saint feast). The cheese counterpart to meat burek.

breakfast.name: Kajmak on Toast
ingredients: Kajmak (Serbian clotted cream -- fresh or aged)
instructions: Kajmak is the Serbian dairy product -- clotted cream made from raw milk
The making of kajmak: raw milk slowly heated, the cream layer skimmed off and salted
The cream is layered in a wooden barrel and aged
Fresh kajmak: white, soft, creamy, milky, slightly salty
Aged kajmak: yellow, firmer, more pungent, intense
Spread on fresh white bread: the simplest Serbian breakfast
Also paired with ajvar (roasted red pepper and eggplant spread)
Kajmak + ajvar on bread: the Balkan combination
Kajmak is made in mountain regions: Zlatibor, Zlatar, Sjenica in southwestern Serbia
The milk of mountain-grazing cattle gives superior kajmak
breakfast.description: Serbian clotted cream on bread -- kajmak made by skimming the cream layer from slowly heated raw milk, salting, and layering in a wooden barrel. Fresh kajmak is white and milky; aged is yellow and pungent. Spread on white bread with optional ajvar (roasted red pepper spread). Made in the mountain regions of southwestern Serbia from the milk of mountain-grazing cattle.

breakfast.name: White Coffee (Bela Kafa)
ingredients: Instant coffee (Nes kafa -- Nescafe, the Serbian norm)
Hot milk (not water -- the Serbian way)
instructions: Bela kafa (white coffee) is the Serbian morning coffee tradition
Serbian coffee culture is split: turska kafa (Turkish coffee -- espresso-strength) and bela kafa
Bela kafa: instant coffee prepared with HOT MILK, not water
The milk-based coffee is lighter, more dairy, less intense
Nescafe (instant coffee) is the standard in Serbian homes for bela kafa
Turkish coffee (turska kafa) is prepared in a dzezva (copper long-handled pot)
The dzezva is placed on the stove, coffee and sugar added, brought to a boil twice
Served with foam in the top -- the foam is the quality indicator of turska kafa
Bela kafa for breakfast; turska kafa after meals and for guests
breakfast.description: Serbian white coffee -- instant coffee (Nescafe) prepared with hot milk instead of water, lighter and more dairy than Turkish coffee. Serbian coffee culture is split: bela kafa (white coffee) for breakfast; turska kafa (Turkish coffee brewed in a dzezva) after meals and for guests. The foam on the Turkish coffee is the quality indicator.

lunch.name: Cevapi (Grilled Minced Meat)
ingredients: Garlic, salt, black pepper, baking soda
Lepinja (flatbread -- the specific Serbian bread for cevapi)
instructions: Cevapi are the grilled minced meat sausages -- the symbol of Balkan food
Shared across the former Yugoslavia: Serbia, Bosnia, Croatia, Montenegro all have cevapi
But the Bosnian cevapi (from Sarajevo) are considered the original reference
The Sarajevo cevapi: small, thin, served in somun (pita) with cream cheese and onion
The Serbian cevapi: slightly larger, served in lepinja (flatbread) with kajmak and ajvar
The meat mix: pure beef, or beef + lamb -- the ratios vary by cook
Baking soda: the Serbian secret ingredient that keeps the cevapi light and tender
Grilled over charcoal or wood fire -- the char is essential
Served on a platter: 5-10 cevapi inside the lepinja with toppings arranged around
The combination: cevapi + kajmak + ajvar + raw onion = the Balkan flavor profile
lunch.description: Serbian-Balkan grilled minced meat sausages -- beef (or beef/lamb) with garlic and baking soda (keeps them tender), grilled over charcoal, served in lepinja flatbread with kajmak, ajvar (roasted red pepper spread), and raw diced onion. Shared across former Yugoslavia but each republic has its variation; Sarajevo cevapi are the regional reference. The Balkan flavor profile in one dish.

lunch.name: Sarma (Stuffed Cabbage Rolls)
ingredients: Sauerkraut (whole fermented cabbage leaves -- or fresh cabbage for summer version)
Smoked pork ribs or tocino (to layer in the pot)
instructions: Sarma is the Serbian national dish -- stuffed fermented cabbage rolls
The sauerkraut cabbage leaves are the essential element: the fermentation adds sourness
Summer sarma uses fresh cabbage leaves; winter sarma uses sauerkraut leaves
The filling: minced pork and beef with rice, onion, and paprika
The rice expands as it cooks -- do not overfill
The rolls are placed in a large pot with smoked pork ribs for flavor
The smoking and the sourness of the sauerkraut are the dominant flavors
Cooked for 2-3 hours over low heat -- the longer the better
Sarma improves the next day: the flavors deepen overnight
At every Serbian celebration: Christmas (Bozic), New Year, Slava, weddings
The whole pig is used: the pork in the filling, the ribs in the pot
lunch.description: Serbian national celebration dish -- minced pork-beef-rice stuffed into fermented sauerkraut leaves (the fermentation sourness is essential) and slow-cooked for 2-3 hours with smoked pork ribs. The smoky-sour combination is the dish. Improves overnight. At every Serbian celebration: Christmas, Slava, weddings, New Year. Summer version uses fresh cabbage leaves.

lunch.name: Srpska Corba (Serbian Soup)
ingredients: Vegetables: carrot, parsnip, celery, leek, onion
instructions: Srpska corba (Serbian soup) is the everyday soup tradition
Corba: the Balkan word for soup (from Turkish corbasi)
Beef corba: a clear beef broth with vegetables and noodles
The broth is fundamental in Serbian cuisine -- long-simmered with bones
The vegetables: the classic corba aromatic base
Vermicelli added near the end -- fine noodles that cook quickly
Finished with fresh parsley and served with sour cream
The sour cream stirred into the hot soup thickens and enriches it
Other Serbian soups: pileca corba (chicken), telecan paprikas (veal with paprika)
Sunday lunch in Serbia traditionally begins with corba
lunch.description: Serbian clear beef broth soup -- beef bones simmered with carrot, parsnip, celery, and leek into a clear golden broth, with vermicelli added near the end, served with fresh parsley and a spoon of sour cream. Sunday lunch in Serbia traditionally begins with corba. The broth is long-simmered; the clarity and depth mark the quality.

lunch.name: Pecenje (Serbian Spit-Roast)
ingredients: Whole pig or lamb (suckling pig is the most festive)
instructions: Pecenje is the Serbian spit-roast -- the most important celebration food
Whole pig (prasice -- suckling pig) or lamb roasted on a wooden spit over open fire
The suckling pig: the classic for Serbian birthdays, Slava, and celebrations
The skin: the most prized element -- it must be crackled, golden, shattering
The technique: the fire must be at the right distance -- not too close (burns the skin), not too far
The turning: the spit is turned continuously (by hand traditionally, motor-assisted today)
Basting with lard: the pig is basted with melted lard for the crispy skin
Cooking time: 3-6 hours depending on size
The whole pig arrives at the table -- carving is a ceremony
The crackling skin first, distributed to everyone -- the most anticipated moment
lunch.description: The Serbian celebration spit-roast -- whole suckling pig or lamb roasted on a wooden spit over open fire for 3-6 hours, basted with lard until the skin crackles golden and shattering. The crackling skin distributed first is the most anticipated moment. Required for Slava (patron saint feast), major birthdays, and weddings. The turning and basting rhythm is a skill passed through families.

lunch.name: Prebranac (Baked Beans)
instructions: Prebranac is the Serbian baked bean dish -- slow-baked in the oven
Different from pasulj (bean soup): prebranac has almost no liquid, it is baked dry
The beans are boiled first, then transferred to a clay or ceramic baking dish
Fried onions and paprika oil are added
Baked in the oven for 1-2 hours until the top caramelizes
The top should develop a golden, slightly crispy layer
The interior: soft, creamy beans with the caramelized onion through
Prebranac is Lenten food in Serbia -- served during Orthodox fasting periods
Also served as a side dish with roasted meat
The Orthodox fasting calendar: Wednesdays and Fridays are meatless in traditional Serbian Orthodox practice
lunch.description: Serbian baked beans -- boiled white beans with caramelized onions and sweet paprika oil, baked in a clay dish until the top develops a golden, slightly crispy layer while the interior remains soft and creamy. Lenten food during Orthodox fasting periods (Wednesdays and Fridays in traditional practice). Also a side dish with roasted meat.

dinner.name: Pasulj (Bean Soup)
instructions: Pasulj is Serbian bean soup -- possibly the most beloved Serbian everyday food
The Serbian saying: cesto pasulj, retko meso (often beans, rarely meat) -- the old peasant reality
Now: pasulj is eaten by choice, not necessity -- it is deeply loved
The beans: soaked overnight, then cooked in fresh water with smoked pork
The smoked pork ribs give the soup its distinctive smoky depth
The paprika paste is made separately -- onion fried in oil with sweet paprika
The paprika paste is added to the soup -- the redness, sweetness, and oil float on top
Pasulj is a one-pot meal -- the beans and smoked meat together
Served with rakija (plum brandy) and fresh bread
The Bosnian version (grah) and the Serbian version (pasulj) are essentially the same
dinner.description: Serbian bean soup -- large white beans simmered with smoked pork ribs and a paprika paste (onion fried in oil with sweet paprika, added to the soup). The smoked pork gives distinctive depth. The Serbian saying: often beans, rarely meat. Now eaten by choice, not necessity; deeply loved. Served with fresh bread. Nearly identical to Bosnian grah across the border.

dinner.name: Musaka (Serbian Moussaka)
ingredients: Minced pork (the Serbian version uses pork, not lamb)
Potatoes (sliced, NOT eggplant -- the Serbian version)
instructions: Serbian musaka is different from Greek moussaka in two ways
First: Serbian musaka uses POTATOES, not eggplant -- completely different vegetable
Second: Serbian musaka uses PORK, not lamb -- different meat
The layers: sliced potatoes alternating with spiced minced pork
Baked in a large pan with layers building up
The top: a simple egg and sour cream custard is poured over
Baked until the custard sets and turns golden
Serbian musaka is homestyle cooking -- at every Serbian family table
The Greek musaka is known internationally; the Serbian version is just as good
dinner.description: Serbian potato musaka -- layers of sliced potatoes alternating with spiced minced pork (NOT eggplant and NOT lamb: two Serbian distinctions from the Greek version), topped with egg and sour cream custard, baked until the custard sets golden. Homestyle family cooking, present at every Serbian table. The Greek version is internationally known; the Serbian version is equally satisfying.

dinner.name: Leskovacki Rostilj (Leskovac Mixed Grill)
ingredients: Rolovana pljeskavica (rolled burger with kajmak inside)
instructions: Leskovacki rostilj is the grilled meat tradition of Leskovac (southern Serbia)
Leskovac: the Serbian city that claims the title of grilled meat capital
The Leskovac grill festival: an annual celebration of Serbian grill culture
The pljeskavica: the Serbian burger -- flat minced meat patty, larger than a regular burger
The rolovana pljeskavica: a rolled pljeskavica with kajmak stuffed inside -- melts while grilling
Kobasice: the Serbian pork sausage
Combined: the Leskovacki plate with cevapi, pljeskavica, and kobasice
Served with lepinja bread, raw onion, ajvar, and kajmak
The charcoal is essential -- gas-grilled Leskovac food is not the same
Leskovac locals say: their cevapi are the real ones, the Bosnian version is imitation
dinner.description: Leskovac (southern Serbia) mixed grill -- cevapi, pljeskavica (flat minced meat burger), rolovana pljeskavica (rolled with kajmak inside), and kobasice (pork sausage) all grilled over charcoal, served with lepinja flatbread, raw onion, ajvar, and kajmak. Leskovac claims the title of Serbian grilled meat capital and hosts an annual grill festival. The charcoal is essential.

dinner.name: Karadjordjeva Snicla (Rolled Veal Schnitzel)
ingredients: Veal or pork escalope (thin, pounded flat)
instructions: Karadjordjeva snicla (Karadjordje schnitzel) is named after the Serbian revolutionary
Karadjordje (Black George): the leader of the First Serbian Uprising against the Ottomans (1804)
The schnitzel is rolled (not flat) -- the kajmak is stuffed inside
The veal (or pork) is pounded thin, kajmak placed in the center, rolled tightly
Breaded: flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs
Fried in hot oil until golden on all sides
When cut, the kajmak melts out from the center
The melting kajmak is the reveal moment
Served with tartar sauce and lemon
The dish was created in the 1950s at the Dva Jelena restaurant in Belgrade
dinner.description: Serbian stuffed schnitzel named after the revolutionary Karadjordje -- pounded veal or pork stuffed with kajmak (Serbian clotted cream), rolled, breaded, and fried until golden. When cut, the kajmak melts from the center. Created in the 1950s at the Dva Jelena restaurant in Belgrade. Served with tartar sauce and lemon.

dinner.name: Podvarak (Roast Meat with Sauerkraut)
ingredients: Sauerkraut (rinsed -- less sour than for sarma)
instructions: Podvarak is the Serbian method of roasting meat on a bed of sauerkraut
The sauerkraut serves as both the cooking medium and the side dish
The sauerkraut is placed in the roasting pan first
The meat goes on top of the sauerkraut
As the meat roasts, the fat renders down into the sauerkraut
The sauerkraut absorbs the rendered fat and meat juices
The result: the sauerkraut becomes soft, slightly fatty, and savory -- not sour
The sourness of the sauerkraut is tamed by the roasting
Podvarak is Christmas and winter food -- the sauerkraut and pork combination
A simple but deeply satisfying Serbian home dinner
dinner.description: Serbian roasted meat on sauerkraut -- pork or chicken placed on a bed of sauerkraut in the roasting pan; the fat renders into the sauerkraut as the meat roasts, making it soft, savory, and slightly fatty. The sourness is tamed by the roasting. Christmas and winter food. The sauerkraut serves as both cooking medium and side dish.

snacks.name: Ajvar (Roasted Red Pepper Spread)
ingredients: Red peppers (horn peppers -- long red peppers, roasted over fire)
instructions: Ajvar is the Serbian roasted red pepper spread -- one of the great condiments
The name comes from the Turkish word for caviar -- the comparison was to the caviar of the poor
Made in autumn when red peppers are at their peak ripeness
The peppers roasted over an open flame or in the oven until blackened
Peeled of their charred skin -- the black skin lifts off easily after cooling
Ground or chopped -- the texture is a choice: chunky or smooth
Cooked down slowly in oil until the moisture evaporates and it thickens
The ajvar-making season: families make large quantities for the winter
Glass jars filled with ajvar: the Serbian pantry staple
Served with cevapi, bread, cheese, eggs -- everything in Serbian cuisine
snacks.description: Serbian roasted red pepper spread -- long red peppers charred over open flame, peeled, chopped or ground, and cooked down in oil until thick. The autumn pepper harvest season is ajvar-making time: families process large quantities into glass jars for winter. Served with cevapi, bread, eggs, cheese -- the universal Serbian condiment. The word comes from Turkish for caviar: the caviar of the poor.

snacks.name: Proja (Cornbread)
ingredients: Optional additions: white cheese, ham, sunflower seeds
instructions: Proja is Serbian cornbread -- a legacy of the Ottoman corn trade
Corn arrived in the Balkans from the Americas via Ottoman trade routes
Proja: a quick, dense, savory cornbread that requires no yeast
The sour cream or yoghurt gives moisture and slight tang
Cheese or ham can be mixed in -- making it more substantial
Baked in a round or square pan -- cut into pieces when warm
Proja is the bread of the Serbian countryside -- cheaper and faster than wheat bread
Served warm with kajmak -- the cornbread + kajmak is a snack combination
Also eaten with beans (pasulj) -- corn and beans, the old Balkan peasant combination
snacks.description: Serbian cornbread -- coarse cornmeal with eggs, oil, and sour cream, baked into a dense, slightly tangy savory bread. Corn arrived in the Balkans via Ottoman trade routes from the Americas. The bread of the Serbian countryside: cheaper and faster than wheat bread. Served warm with kajmak, or alongside pasulj (bean soup).

snacks.name: Rakija (Plum Brandy)
ingredients: Rakija (Serbian fruit brandy -- most commonly slivovitz: plum brandy)
instructions: Rakija is the Serbian national drink -- fruit brandy, most commonly plum (slivovitz)
Slivovica (slivovitz): from sliva = plum in Serbian
Serbia is the world largest producer of plums -- much of the plum crop becomes rakija
Home distillation of rakija is a Serbian tradition -- almost every village family makes it
The rakija still (alembic): a family heirloom in Serbian villages
The first pressing (prepechenica) has higher alcohol -- the strong version
The second pressing: more refined, more balanced
Rakija is drunk at every Serbian occasion: breakfast, welcome drink, toast, after meals
The Serbian greeting: dobrodo slo (welcome) and a glass of rakija
Loza (grape), kajsija (apricot), kruska (pear): other rakija varieties
snacks.description: Serbia national spirit -- fruit brandy, most commonly slivovitz (plum brandy: Serbia is the world largest plum producer). Home distillation is a Serbian tradition; almost every village family has a rakija still. Drunk at every Serbian occasion from breakfast to bedtime. The Serbian welcome drink. First pressing (prepechenica) is stronger; second pressing more refined. Loza (grape), kajsija (apricot), and kruska (pear) are other varieties.

imageCredit.author: The original uploader was Blue at Bulgarian Wikipedia.

snacks.name: Pita (Serbian Phyllo Roll)
ingredients: Filling: white cheese, eggs, and cream
instructions: Serbian pita is the rolled phyllo pastry -- different from burek (coiled) in shape
Pita = rolled in a log shape; burek = coiled in a spiral
The cheese pita: crumbled white cheese, eggs, cream
The zeljanica (spinach pita): spinach and cheese
Rolled into a log and baked until golden
Cut into slices for serving
The pekara (bakery) in Serbia sells all varieties side by side
Each filling has its name: sirnica (cheese), zeljanica (spinach), krompirusa (potato)
snacks.description: Serbian rolled phyllo pastry -- yufka (phyllo) sheets filled with white cheese and eggs (or spinach and cheese), rolled into a log and baked until golden, cut into slices. Different from burek which is coiled in a spiral. Each filling has its name: sirnica (cheese), zeljanica (spinach), krompirusa (potato). The pekara sells all varieties side by side.

desserts.name: Krofna (Serbian Doughnut)
ingredients: Dough: flour, milk, butter, sugar, egg yolks, yeast
Jam filling (rose hip, apricot, or plum)
instructions: Krofna are Serbian doughnuts -- the Balkan version of the Central European Krapfen
The name from German Krapfen -- the Austro-Hungarian influence on Serbian cuisine
Vojvodina (northern Serbia): the most Austro-Hungarian influenced Serbian region
The dough is enriched -- egg yolks make it rich and golden
Fried until deep golden -- the interior should be pillow-soft
Filled with jam after frying -- a piping bag injects the jam into the center
Rose hip jam (sipurak): the traditional Serbian filling
Apricot or plum jam: also common Serbian fillings
Dusted with icing sugar -- the white snow on the golden krofna
Krofna season: winter and carnival (poklade/fasnik)
desserts.description: Serbian doughnuts -- enriched yeast dough (egg yolks make them golden and rich), deep-fried until pillow-soft, filled with rose hip jam (sipurak) or apricot jam via piping bag, dusted with icing sugar. From the Austro-Hungarian Krapfen tradition: Vojvodina (northern Serbia) is the most Austro-Hungarian influenced region. Winter and carnival season.

desserts.name: Tufahije (Poached Apple with Walnut Cream)
ingredients: Whole apples (peeled, cored from the bottom -- kept whole)
Walnut filling: ground walnuts, sugar, vanilla, rum
instructions: Tufahije are the Bosnian-Serbian poached apple dessert -- Ottoman-heritage
The name from Arabic tuffaha (apple)
Ottoman-era dessert: the walnut-stuffed poached apple was a classic Ottoman sweet
The apples are cored from the bottom -- the top stays intact
Poached in sweet syrup until just tender but still holding their shape
The walnuts: ground and mixed with sugar, vanilla, and a little rum
The walnut paste fills the apple cavity
Served with whipped cream poured over
The apple should be tender but not falling apart -- the timing is everything
Tufahije is shared across the former Yugoslavia -- each country claims it
desserts.description: Serbian-Bosnian Ottoman poached apple dessert -- whole apples cored from the bottom, poached in sugar syrup until just tender (still holding shape), filled with ground walnut-sugar-vanilla paste, served with whipped cream. From Arabic tuffaha (apple); an Ottoman court dessert that survived across the Balkans. Shared across former Yugoslavia: each country claims it as their own.

desserts.name: Vanilice (Crescent Cookies)
ingredients: Raspberry or apricot jam (for the filling)
instructions: Vanilice are Serbian crescent cookies -- the Christmas cookie
The name: vanil = vanilla -- the vanilla flavor is the identity
Made with a mix of butter and lard -- the lard makes them more crumbly
Ground walnuts mixed into the dough -- the walnut-vanilla combination
Shaped into crescents (the typical shape) or rounds
Baked gently -- they should not brown, just dry out slightly
Sandwiched with jam between two cookies (or left single)
Rolled in vanilla icing sugar immediately after baking while still warm
Every Serbian grandmother makes vanilice for Christmas
The Christmas cookie table: vanilice alongside cevapcici cookies and others
desserts.description: Serbian Christmas crescent cookies -- butter and lard dough (lard makes them crumbly) mixed with finely ground walnuts and vanilla sugar, shaped into crescents, baked until just dried (not browned), optionally sandwiched with jam, and rolled in vanilla icing sugar while still warm. Every Serbian grandmother makes vanilice for Christmas.

drinks.name: Turska Kafa (Serbian Turkish Coffee)
ingredients: Finely ground coffee (very fine -- Turkish grind)
instructions: Turska kafa (Turkish coffee) is the Serbian coffee tradition
Called Turkish coffee everywhere in the Balkans -- a source of tension since the Kosovo war
Made in a dzezva (copper or stainless long-handled pot)
Cold water and coffee measured into the dzezva -- then placed on heat
The coffee is brought to a near-boil -- the foam rises
The key: remove before it boils over, let the foam subside, heat again
Served in a small fildzanka (demitasse-style cup)
The foam on top is the quality indicator -- a good kafa has good foam
Sugar: put in during cooking (slah = very sweet, srednje = medium, bez = no sugar)
The coffee grounds settle -- you drink until the grounds, not through them
Drunk slowly, with conversation -- the kafana (coffee shop) culture
drinks.description: Serbian Turkish coffee -- finely ground coffee brewed in a dzezva (copper long-handled pot), brought to a near-boil twice to build foam, served in small fildzanke cups. The foam quality indicates the brew quality. Sugar is put in during cooking (slah: very sweet, srednje: medium, bez: none). Drunk slowly in kafana (coffee shops). The coffee grounds settle; drink until you reach them.

drinks.name: Sljivovica (Plum Brandy)
ingredients: Sljivovica (rakija from plums -- Serbia national spirit)
instructions: Sljivovica is the specific plum rakija -- the Serbian national identity spirit
Serbia produces approximately 2 million tons of plums annually -- many become sljivovica
The plums: Pozegaca (Stanley-type) or Crvena ranka -- local Serbian plum varieties
Double-distilled sljivovica (prepechenica): the stronger, more refined version
Aged sljivovica: gold-colored from time in oak barrels -- more complex
The Serbian toast: ziveli! (to life)
Served in small shot glasses or little tulip glasses
Room temperature (NOT cold) -- the aroma opens at room temperature
The Sremska Mitrovica sljivovica festival: the celebration of plum brandy culture
Sljivovica is also used medicinally in Serbia: for a cold, for a stomachache, for a wound
drinks.description: Serbia national plum spirit -- the double-distilled version (prepechenica) is stronger and more refined; aged in oak is gold-colored and complex. Served at room temperature (not cold: the aroma opens). Serbian toast: ziveli! (to life). Serbia produces approximately 2 million tons of plums annually, many becoming sljivovica. Also used medicinally: for a cold, a stomachache, or a wound.

drinks.name: Sok od Zove (Elderflower Juice)
ingredients: Fresh elderflowers (Sambucus nigra -- white flowers, late May to June)
instructions: Sok od zove (elderflower juice) is the Serbian summer drink
Elderflower season: late May to early June -- when the white flowers appear
The flowers are collected and steeped with lemon and sugar in cold water
Left to infuse for 24-48 hours -- the color turns pale yellow-green
Strained, sweetened further, and bottled
The flavor: floral, slightly musky, summery -- unlike anything else
Every Serbian family has an elderflower juice tradition
The homemade juice keeps for weeks in the refrigerator
Elderflower syrup for diluting with water throughout the summer
drinks.description: Serbian elderflower juice -- fresh white elderflowers steeped with lemon and sugar in cold water for 24-48 hours until pale yellow-green, strained and bottled. The flavor is floral, slightly musky, and distinctly summery. Every Serbian family makes it in late May to June. Homemade elderflower syrup diluted with water throughout the summer.
